structure.title: 2. Overview (binary case, survey of IV specifications, implications for practice)
3. Definition and characterization of weakly causal estimands
5. Alternatives to linear IV (incl. 5.4 Monte Carlo simulation)
6. Applications (Card; two modern applications; patterns from multiple studies)
Acknowledgments, Supplementary Data, Data Availability, Funding, References

observations.statement: The paper defines the IV estimand as a population coefficient via Frisch-Waugh-Lovell and states conditional exogeneity and monotonicity as named assumptions before any decomposition result.

A minimal causal criterion (weakly causal) is defined abstractly, separate from the functional form of the estimand, and then specialised to TSLS; assumptions carry labels (EXO, MON, RC, CLE, LIN) used throughout.
observations.locator: Sections 3.2 and 4.2, Definition WC, Definition RC, Theorem 1

observations.statement: Choice groups (never-takers, compliers, always-takers, defiers) are defined from potential treatments, and the paper explains that decompositions of the estimand into group effects are not unique without rich covariates.
Relation to the two-way fixed effects heterogeneity literature is discussed in a footnote to position the contribution (level dependence versus negative weights).

The literature survey sample is built by a Web of Science keyword search over a stated date window in five named journals; exclusions (methodological papers, other meanings of instrument) are explained and counts by journal are tabulated.

For the multi-study reanalysis, inclusion requires available data, successful replication of the main IV estimate, a single endogenous variable with a single excluded instrument, and no two-way fixed effects panels; each restriction is justified.

Each reanalysed application is introduced with its data source, unit, outcome, treatment, instrument and the original table and column being reproduced; sample sizes and number of included variables appear as rows of the comparison table.

Outcome, treatment and instrument for each application are restated in words (log wage, years of schooling, college proximity; trust, log of one plus exports, distance to coast; war indicator, queen indicator, firstborn male indicator).
The full covariate list of each original specification is enumerated and the original authors' stated reason for including covariates (instrument exogeneity) is quoted with page reference.

The simulation DGP is calibrated to a real dataset: the instrument propensity is an interacted cubic polynomial fit to the data, treatment probabilities match empirical counterparts, and outcomes are generated by an optimisation matching several estimates while imposing linearity.

The main application table stacks estimators as rows (OLS, IV without covariates, IV with covariates, DDML PLIV, Abadie kappa, DDML and IPSW LATE/ACR) with columns per application, plus RESET p-value, relative bias ratios, outcome and treatment means, covariate count and N.
For one application the paper reports variants dropping polity fixed effects or the previous-monarch controls in a supplementary table to show how much covariates matter.
Every IV estimate is reported alongside a comparable OLS estimate defined as instrumenting the treatment with itself, used later as a benchmark for the size of specification bias.
Standard errors are heteroskedasticity or cluster robust depending on the original application; the choice follows each replicated paper rather than being justified anew.
observations.locator: Section 6 opening paragraph and footnote 11; Table 3 notes
observations.quote: heteroskedasticity and/or cluster-robust depending on the original application

observations.statement: DDML estimates are the median across many random cross-fitting splits (fewer splits in simulations, more in applications), and standard errors include an adjustment for uncertainty over splits, citing the DDML source.
Standard errors for the kappa weighting and IPSW estimators are block bootstrapped, with the tails of the bootstrap distribution trimmed for kappa; this is stated in the table notes.

A Ramsey RESET test of the regression of the instrument on covariates is run for every application as the test of rich covariates; implementation uses second and third powers of fitted values, stated in a footnote.

Estimated instrument propensities are trimmed to an interior interval for one application when used in kappa weighting and IPSW, disclosed in the table notes; a logit is used to estimate the propensity.

The implicit weights on compliers and always-takers implied by the IV estimand are plotted by covariate cell in the simulation DGP, with negative weights shaded; the alternative complier/never-taker decomposition is relegated to a supplementary figure.
observations.locator: Figure 2 and its notes; Figure SA.2

observations.statement: The Monte Carlo compares five estimators across sample sizes and covariate support sizes, reporting trimmed means, standard deviations relative to a correctly specified benchmark, and RMSE in faceted figures; detailed numbers go to supplementary tables.
observations.locator: Section 5.4, Figures 3 and 4, Tables SA.1 and SA.2

observations.statement: Alternative ML learners (single expressive algorithms, lasso) are examined in a supplementary table and discussed as a bias-versus-risk tradeoff relative to the ensemble.
The multi-study comparison is shown as a two-panel bar figure with bars shaded by whether the RESET test rejects; per-study tabular results and sample details are in supplementary tables.
observations.locator: Section 6.3, Figure 5, Tables SA.4 and SA.5

observations.statement: Differences between IV and DDML estimates are expressed as two ratios: relative to the original IV estimate and relative to the OLS versus DDML gap (specification versus selection bias); both are defined in table notes.
The text repeatedly compares the precision of DDML estimates with the original IV standard errors and notes when a re-estimate is no longer distinguishable from zero at conventional levels.
A hand-computable numerical example with a three-point covariate is used to make the weights and sign reversal concrete, and a single figure plots the estimand against the always-taker effect.

The authors stress that the weakly causal criterion is extremely weak and that estimands can coincide numerically even when only one has a causal interpretation, cautioning against over-reading small IV versus DDML gaps.

One study where the RESET test fails to detect a large gap is attributed to a tiny sample and likely low power; noisy kappa and IPSW estimates are attributed to many fixed effects making the logit hard to estimate.

Statements about estimators are flagged as being about estimands only, not finite-sample statistical properties; the theory is stated for discrete supports with extension to continuous cases described as routine.
Tables report standard errors in parentheses without significance stars; notes define bias ratios, bootstrap procedures, trimming and why some cells are missing (non-binary instrument).
Survey tables show both percentages and raw counts per journal, with a final All row, and a note explaining which subset of papers the second table classifies.

Supplementary material is labelled SA (figures SA.1 to SA.3, tables SA.1 to SA.5); simulation figure notes state the number of draws, trimming of tails, exclusion of undefined draws and changing axis scales.
observations.locator: Figures 3 and 4 notes; references to SA items

observations.statement: The introduction previews each section's result in order and closes with a paragraph contrasting the contribution with the closest related work (Kolesar, Sloczynski).
A binary-case overview with intuition, numerical example and survey precedes the general theory; the paper quotes the textbook claims it challenges verbatim with page numbers.
The conclusion gives a numbered step-by-step protocol for practitioners, naming the Stata command and R function for the RESET test and the packages for DDML and IPSW.

Proofs are placed in an appendix; generalisations (stratified assignment, multiple excluded variables, weaker monotonicity, DGP details) are deferred to a supplementary appendix and pointed to in footnotes and text.
A Data Availability paragraph states that data and code are on Zenodo with a DOI; supplementary data are on the journal site.
Software is named in footnotes: simulations in R with the ddml package and gbm, nnet, ranger, glmnet back ends; applications in Stata with ddml and pystacked calling scikit-learn.

The ML ensemble is fully specified (random forest with tree count and split variables, boosted trees with stage count, neural net with neuron count) and the stacking rule (short-stacking with non-negative least squares) is cited.
Empirical inputs are existing survey and replication datasets of published studies (NLSY based Card data, Afrobarometer based data, European polity panel); studies without available data are dropped.

Gaps between DDML PLIV and unconditional LATE estimates are interpreted through the theoretical weighting difference derived earlier, and a second independent estimator (IPSW) is used to corroborate the DDML LATE.

Generality of the empirical point is argued by systematically reanalysing all eligible papers from the survey rather than only hand-picked examples, and by contrasting detection and non-detection cases.
The handling editor is named on the title page and funding sources with grant numbers are listed at the end.

gaps: No independent justification for the clustering level; SEs simply follow each original study.
No first-stage or weak-instrument statistics are reported for the reanalysed applications.
No multiple-testing adjustment is discussed for testing across thirteen studies.
The supplementary appendix (SA sections) is not included in the text file, so DGP details and SA tables could not be read.
No preregistration or ethics statement (not applicable).
